title: Lecture 3b – Goitre, nodules, thyroid cancer, thyroiditis
html:
Source: CursIII-MGE noduli si tiroidite 2023.pptx – 31 slides

THE THYROID GLAND #1

NONTOXIC DIFFUSE GOITER AND NODULAR THYROID DISEASE and Thyroid NODULES and Thyroid cancer #2

Goiter= enlargement of the thyroid gland #3

  • Nontoxic goiter (ie, goiter not associated with hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism)
  • -can be diffuse or nodular.
  • Toxic multinodular goiter or nodule
  • Thyroid nodules are extremely common; ♀
  • The prevalence of palpable nodule - 4 % of adult population (USA)
  • thyroid nodules are detected on thyroid ultrasound in up to 50% of healthy individuals
  • <5% are cancerous;
  • Although thyroid nodules are common, thyroid cancer is a relatively rare condition –with an annual incidence of thyroid cancer ≈8.7 per 100.000 population
  • Multinodular goiter-nodular thyroid swelling which may be associated with hyperthyroidsim and is not auto-immune in origin

Slide 4 #4

Etiology of goiter:
Autoimmune thyroid disease (Hashimoto’s thyroiditis)
Subacute thyroiditis
Endemic (iodine deficiency, dietary origins) Endemic goiter is an iodine-deficiency disease (IDD) that occurs in those areas where the iodine content of the soil is so low that insufficient iodine is obtained through food and water and occurs when no provision is made for supplying iodized salt.
Sporadic
Congenital Causes of Goiter: (dyshormonogenesis) This rare condition is due to genetic defects in the synthesis of thyroid hormones; patients develop hypothyroidism with goitre. One particular familial form is associated with sensorineural deafness due to a deletion mutation in chromosome 7, causing a defect of the transporter pendrin (Pendred’s syndrome)
Thyroid neoplasm- benign or malignant
Drug-induced (ATDs, lithium, amiodarone, TKI, checkpoint inhibitors).

Causes of thyroid nodules #5

  • Causes of thyroid nodules
BENIGNMALIGNANT
Multinodular (sporadic) goiter ("colloid adenoma") (colloid-filled or hyperplastic cellular nodules (dominant nodule) within a multinodular goiter) Hashimoto's (chronic lymphocytic) thyroiditis Cysts (colloid, simple, or hemorrhagic) Benign adenoma ( Follicular, Huthle cell) Rare: lipoma, hemangioma, teratoma1.Papillary carcinoma (80%) 2.Follicular carcinoma (including Hurthle cell carcinoma) 10% = differentiated thyroid cancers Medullary carcinoma 5% Undifferentiated (anaplastic) carcinoma 3% Miscellaneous (including lymphoma, metastatic carcinoma: breast, renal etc) 1%

PATHOGENESIS : The role of genetic factors. Some goiters are due to mutations in genes involved in thyroid growth and/or thyroid function, as suggested by the clustering of goiters within families. → a complex network of both TSH-dependent and TSH-independent pathways plays a role in the goitrogenic process. Iodine Deficiency (endemic goiter) and Congenital Causes of Goiter Optimal iodine requirements for adults:150-300g/day. In endemic goiter areas the daily intake (and urinary excretion) of iodine falls <50 g/day→ the gland is unable to maintain adequate hormonal secretion, and thyroid hypertrophy ( goiter) and hypothyroidism result. endocrine disrupters, including perchlorate, thiocyanate, and nitrate; isoflavones; and organochlorines→ in goiter development ! The mechanism for the development of autonomous growth and function of thyroid nodules may involve some activating mutations in the TSH rec (Gs protein in the cell membrane) which result in thyroid cell proliferation and hyperfunction even when TSH is suppressed. The most common cause of thyroid enlargement in developed countries is chronic thyroiditis (Hashimoto’s thyroiditis) →gene mutations producing a benign lesion, such as adenoma, or to a malignant one, such as carcinoma #6

Diagnostic approach #7

  • Initial evaluation
  • History and physical examination
  • ●Measurement of serum TSH
  • ●Ultrasound to confirm the presence of nodularity, assess sonographic features, and assess for the presence of additional nodules and lymphadenopathy

Slide 8 #8

  • History + clinical examination should concentrate on risk factors that predispose to benign or malignant disease:
  • Individuals at higher risk of thyroid cancer
  • • A previous history of radiation, especially childhood head and neck irradiation.
  • • A family history of papillary or medullary carcinoma (MEN 2 sdr ).
  • • The development of hoarseness or dysphagia, history of recent thyroid growth.
  • • Nodules are more likely to be malignant in patients <20 or >60 years.
  • • Thyroid nodules are more common in ♀ but more likely to be malignant in ♂.
  • • Physical findings suggestive of malignancy include a solitary firm or hard, non-tender nodule/ a dominant nodule in a multinodular goiter that is clearly different from the rest of the gland, fixation to adjacent tissue, and the presence of suspicious regional lymphadenopathy.
  • .• History of Hashimoto’s disease (↑ incidence of lymphoma).
  • Clinical features associated with a lower risk of thyroid cancer include middle age, female sex, a soft thyroid nodule on physical examination the presence of a multinodular goiter and a family history of goiter

CLINICAL PICTURE thyroid enlargement ( grades I-IV): diffuse or multinodular - pressure symptoms: large, huge goiter which may displace or compress adjacent structures such as trachea, esophagus, neck vessels →rarely associated with dyspnea, inspiratory stridor, dysphagia, chocking sensation, neck tightness or discomfort facial flushing and dilatation of cervical veins on lifting the arms over the head (positive Pemberton sign ← obstruction to jugular venous flow) - invasion or compression of the recurrent laryngeal nerve, causing hoarseness, rarely occurs, though, when present, it suggests advanced thyroid carcinoma. The vast majority of patients are euthyroid; endogenous subclinical thyrotoxicosis caused by autonomously nodules may develop. #9

WHO staging of goiter: #10

  • Grade 1= small goiter; it can’t be observed with the head in a normal position (only with the head in hyperextension), but it can be palpated
  • Grade 2=moderate goiter; physical examination: visible with the head in normal position, palpable; it does not extend beyond the external branch of sternocleidomastoid muscle
  • Grade 3=large goiter: one or both lobes extend beyond the external branch of sternocleidomastoid muscle; it is visible from 10 m distance; ± pressure symptoms in the neck
  • Grade 4= huge goiter; extend inferiorly to present as substernal goiter and superiorly towards the mandible; it totally deforms the neck and it can be “seen” from behind ; it is accompanied by important pressure symptoms in the neck

SERUM FACTORS #11

  • Hormonal determinations: TSH, FT4 are usually normal
  • Serum TSH is an independent risk factor for predicting malignancy in a thyroid nodule.
  • !!! when cancer was diagnosed, a higher TSH was associated with a more advanced stage of cancer
  • Thyroid autoantibodies: TPO Ab, Tg Ab- a high titer suggests chronic thyroiditis as the cause of thyroid enlargement and nodules, but does not rule out an associated malignancy
  • Measurement of serum calcitonin- an ↑ serum calcitonin in patients with a family history of medullary carcinoma strongly suggests the presence of medullary thyroid cancer
  • Thyroglobulin (Tg) is a protein produced by normal thyroid cells and thyroid cancer cells.
  • !!!!! it does not diagnose thyroid cancer when the thyroid gland is still present.
  • It is used most often in patients who have had surgery for thyroid cancer in order to monitor them after treatment.

IMAGING STUDIES #12

  • Ultrasonographic evaluation is the optimal means of evaluating the thyroid gland, goiter, nodules.
  • Clinical Utility of Neck Ultrasound:
  • Thyroid gland: size, volume, characteristics
  • Nodules : number and characteristics of each nodule: diameters, shape, echogenicity, composition, limits, presence of calcifications, vascularization; differentiates solid from cystic nodules
  • Lymph node compartments
  • ####Patients presenting with a palpable thyroid nodule is a common clinical dilemma.###
  • The ultimate aim in the management of a thyroid nodule is to identify patients in whom the nodule is malignant and would benefit from early aggressive treatment while avoiding unnecessary investigation and surgery in the majority of patients who have a benign nodule!!!
  • Certain features of nodules are more common in malignant lesions (eg, hypoechogenicity, microcalcifications, irregular margins, central vascularity, incomplete halo; see also later), and other features are typical of benign lesions (eg, iso- or hyperechogenicity, a spongiform appearance and cystic change)
  • but none of these features can be considered definitive
  • Helps select nodules for FNA
  • Sonography can be used to guide fine-needle aspiration of thyroid nodules.
  • Sequential scanning (follow-up) can be employed to assess changes in size of thyroid and thyroid nodules over time

Subsequent evaluation — #13

  • Subsequent evaluation is based upon the TSH level and sonographic features of the nodule(s)

Slide 14 #14

  • The serum TSH is an independent risk factor for thyroid cancer, with the risk of cancer ↑ progressively with serum TSH levels still within the normal range
  • The sonographic features that are associated with a higher risk of malignancy include solid hypoechoic nodule, microcalcifications, irregular borders (infiltrative, microlobulated) and a „taller than wide „ configuration.
  • Other ultrasound characteristics, such as hyperechogenicity, a thin sonolucent rim („halo”) around the nodule, or a large cystic component favor a benign nodule.
  • A serum TSH should be the initial laboratory study
  • Thyroid ultrasound has become the most important tool
  • > than a radionuclide scan
  • Management of a thyroid nodule
  • nodule is hot or autonomously functioning (and suppressing the remainder of gland
  • = almost never malignant
  • Cold nodule
  • although 5% to 10% of cold nodules may be malignant, 90% to 95% of cold nodules are benign
  • Observe to detect future overt hyperthyroidism

SCINTIGRAPHY (ISOTOPE SCANNING) #15

  • Thyroid scintigraphy is used to determine the functional status of a nodule
  • → a patchy uptake, frequently with focal areas of ↑ uptake corresponding to “hot” nodules and areas of ↓ uptake → “cold” nodule
  • Most thyroid carcinomas are inefficient in trapping and organifying iodine and appear on scans as areas of diminished isotope uptake, referred to as a cold nodule ( !!!10% of surgically removed cold nodule= malignant).
  • Unfortunately, most benign nodules also do not concentrate iodine ( are „cold”) →because both most benign and malignant thyroid nodules are cold, or hypofunctioning, documenting this is not particularly helpful  confirms the limited utility of thyroid scintigraphy in identifying cancerous nodules.
  • On the contrary, a hot (functioning) nodule (takes up more radioactive material than surrounding thyroid tissue) on a radioisotope scan with markedly suppressed or absent uptake in the remainder of the gland suggests a toxic adenoma and makes malignancy less likely. These lesions are typically associated with a suppressed/↓↓ serum TSH level.
  • RAIU: depending on the iodide pool and TSH levels
  • –normal or /↑ (high iodine uptake- in endemic regions) (=Iodine avidity, not hyperthyroidism!!!) /or ↓
  • Neck and mediastinal CT/MRI: in the presence of intrathoracic goiter to define the relationship with surrounding structures

Slide 16 #16

  • If the serum TSH concentration is normal or elevated and the nodule meets sonographic criteria for sampling
  • of a thyroid nodule: in malignity suspicion
  • Diagnostic smears are conventionally subclassified into benign, indeterminate, or malignant categories (the 2017 Bethesda System for Reporting Thyroid Cytopathology has a 6-category classification (see later))
  • !!!!!The major problem = to rule out cancer
  • - it may have therapeutically utility (eg. draining a cyst).
  • FNAB (FINE NEEDLE ASPIRATION BIOPSY/CYTOLOGY)

FNAB: #17

  • The 2017 Bethesda System for Reporting Thyroid Cytopathology has a 6-category classification:
  • nondiagnostic or unsatisfactory;
  • (ii) benign;
  • (iii) atypia of undetermined significance (AUS) or follicular lesion of undetermined significance (FLUS);
  • (iv) follicular neoplasm or suspicious for a follicular neoplasm; (
  • v) suspicious for malignancy; and
  • (vi) malignant
  • If the nodule is cytologically malignant or if the reading is „ suspicious for malignancy” the patient is generally referred for thyroid surgery
  • + thyroxine for life with maintenance of low normal/suppressed serum TSH
  • + radioiodine therapy (131 I) given to most intermediate and all high-risk patients with differentiated thyroid cancers
  • If the nodule is cytologically benign and neither local compressive symptoms nor hyperthyroidism are present, only reassessment of nodule size in 6-18 months by physical examination and/or ultrasound is required.
  • Management of a thyroid nodule

SURGICAL TREATMENT + for goiters that produce obstructive symptoms, with substernal extension A positive or suspicious FNAB makes surgery mandatory, and surgery may be necessary if doubt persists, even in the presence of a negative FNA For goiter that continues to grow despite TSH suppression with LT4 PREVENTION IODIDE for risk groups : pregnancy, lactation, ages: 6-14 and 14-18 #18

Management of nontoxic goiter (diffuse or nodular) Monitoring of nodules that do not meet FNA criteria #19

  • With the exception of those due to neoplasm, nontoxic goiters- simply observation
  • MEDICAL TREATEMENT :in diffuse goiter and nontoxic multinodular goiter ( after excluding malignity)
  • IODIDE (JODID® 100-200 µg/day)
  • L-T4 25-50 mg/day (= suppressive therapy)
  • thyroid hormone supplementation (termed suppressive therapy) →↓TSH→ “reduce” the size of nontoxic goiters.
  • Of note! Pharmacologic doses of iodides (in the forms of amiodarone, radiocontrast agents) may induce either hyperthyroidism in patients with autonomous thyroid nodules or hypothyroidism.
  • PREVENTION
  • IODIDE for risk groups : pregnancy, lactation, ages: 6-14 and 14-18

THYROIDITIS #20

THYROIDITIS CLASSIFICATIONCLASIFICAREA TIROIDITELOR #21

  • 1. ACUTE thyroiditis
  • 2. SUBACUTE thyroiditis
  • 3. CHRONIC thyroiditis
  • Autoimmune
  • Fibrous

ACUTE THYROIDITIS (THYROID ABSCESS ) #22

  • =acute bacterial inflammation of thyroid gland which untreated → abscess
  • Etiology: staphylococcus, streptococcus, gram negative bacteria, fungus
  • rare; may appear in the context of septicemia or acute infective endocarditis or from local extension of a pharyngeal infection
  • Acute onset
  • Clinic
  • GENERAL signs : malaise, fever, sweating
  • LOCAL signs : pain and tenderness, swelling,
  • warmth and redness of the underlying skin
  • Satellite adenopathy
  • ♂ 11 years

LABORATORY FINDINGS #23

  • ↑↑ ESR
  • FBC- anemia, ↑ neutrophils
  • Thyroid ultrasonography : → the abscess or evidence of a hypoechoic solid area
  • Needle aspiration will confirm the diagnosis and identify the organism
  • TREATMENT
  • ANTIBIOTIC THERAPY ± occasionally EXCISION/ DRAINAGE (ABSCESS)
  • A thyroglossal duct cyst may become infected and present as acute suppurative thyroiditis. This too responds to antibiotic therapy and occasionally incision and drainage.

SUBACUTE THYROIDITIS (DE QUERVAIN’ S THYROIDITIS) #24

  • or granulomatous thyroiditis; = an acute inflammatory disorder of the thyroid gland most likely due to viral infection : mumps, adenoviruses, coxsackievirus
  • CLINIC
  • Subacute onset ; usually- !an episode of upper respiratory tract infection in the previous weeks
  • Pain, soreness in the neck, which may extend up to the angle of jaw or toward the ear lobes on one or both sides of the neck
  • Thyroid enlargement, exquisite tenderness and “nodularity of the thyroid gland”
  • Initially, the patient may have symptoms of hyperthyroidism: palpitation, agitation, sweats
  • General signs: pronounced asthenia, fever, malaise, arthralgia
  • → women, individuals who are HLABw5 positive

LABORATORY FINDINGS ↑ ESR (sometimes =100mm/h)/CRP Initially :↑ FT3,FT4 + ↓TSH + ↓↓ RAIU; as the disease progress –FT3,FT4 will ↓ and TSH will ↑( and symptoms of hypothyroidism are noted ); later RAIU ↑ (→ recovery of the gland from the acute insult) Thyroid ultrasonography –hypoechoic aspect corresponding to the affected area TREATMENT In many cases-only symptomatic treatment (aspirin/other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) Prednisone 50-60 mg/day, 7-10 days, then decreasing progressively the dosage -blocker sedative L-thyroxine – during the hypothyroid phase #25

Thyroid ultrasonography #26

  • –hypoechoic aspect corresponding to the affected area

CHRONIC THYROIDITIS (HASHIMOTO’S THYROIDITIS, LYMPHOCYTIC THYROIDITIS ) #27

  • The most common cause of hypothyroidism and goiter
  •  an immunological disorder in which lymphocytes become sensitized to thyroidal antigens and autoantibodies are formed that react with these antigens
  • Pathology : heavy infiltration of lymphocites totally destroiyng normal
  • thyroidal architecture
  • CLINIC
  • Painless, variably –sized goiter with rubbery consistency /small, atrophic thyroid gland
  • Euthyroid / mild hypothyroidism →severe
  • occasionally- “HASHITOXICOSIS ”→ may go through periods of activity when large amounts of fT3,fT4 are released or “ dumped”, resulting in transient symptoms of thyrotoxicosis ( =“spontaneously resolving hyperthyroidism )
  • ! One variant of Hashimoto’s thyroiditis has been termed “silent” or “painless” thyroiditis/postpartum thyroiditis (→ predilection: the postpartum period) ; evolves with a triphasic course, similar to what is seen in subacute thyroiditis :
  • mild hyperthyroidism (1-3 months)→ hypothyroid phase (several months) →recovery
  • ! Reccurent episodes

CHRONIC THYROIDITIS (HASHIMOTO’S THYROIDITIS) #28

  • LABORATORY FINDINGS
  • TSH, fT3, fT4 vary with the course of disease; usually normal/ ↑ TSH ± ↓ T3,T4 / ↓ TSH, ↑T3,T4
  • TPO Abs , Tg Abs  =the most striking laboratory findings
  • ESR=normal
  • Thyroid ultrasonography: diffuse hypoechoic aspect ← Ly infiltrate
  • COMPLICATIONS: progressive hypothyroidism →MYXEDEMA
  • COURSE and PROGNOSIS : may develop other autoimmune diseases: pernicious anemia, adrenal insufficiency, DM type1; may also develop true Graves disease, ocasionally with severe ophtalmopathy or dermopathy
  • TREATMENT
  • Replacement treatment with LT4 – overt hypothyroidism and also subclinical hypothyroidism
  • B-blocker –hyperthyroid phase of silent or postpartum thyroiditis

RIEDEL’ THYROIDITIS #29

  •  rare
  • → characterized by fibrosis of the thyroid gland and adjacent structure
  • CLINIC
  • insidious onset
  • goiter –usually as stony-hard mass with extensive fibrosis extending outside the gland and involving overlying muscle and surrounding tissue
  • compression signs of adjacent structure : TRACHEA, ESOPHAGUS and LARYNGEAL NERVES
  • Euthyroid /mild hypothyroidism
  • surgery may be required to preserve tracheal and esophageal function
  • ! Must be differentiated from thyroid cancer

Drug induced thyroiditis ( → thyroiditis: autoimmue/ distructive ) •Amiodarone may precipitate AITD in susceptible individuals, most likely by increasing Tg iodination and enhancing its immunogenicity. • Lithium. • Interferon alfa or Interleukin 2 (→chronic hepatitis C or various malignancies) . Anticancer drugs SE -induce inflammation and autoimmunity -tyrosine kinase inhibitors: nilotinib ( eg, thyrotoxicosis due to destructive thyroiditis), sunitinib -immune checkpoint inhibitors (immunotherapy drugs) (e.g., immune checkpoint blockade can lead to the breaking of immune self-tolerance, thereby inducing a novel syndrome of autoimmune/autoinflammatory side effects, designated as “immune-related adverse events,” including endocrinopathies - most commonly hypophysitis, more rarely thyroid disease and occasionally primary adrenal insufficiency) #30
